Addition and Multiplication Tables in Various Bases

Place ValueArithmeticAlgebra
Game: See the addition and times tables written in other number systems, and hunt for the patterns that stay the same in all of them.
How to play: Pick + or × and a base. Click a cell, or use the arrow keys, to see what it says.
Look for the math

"Many children grow superstitious, and think that you cannot carry except in tens," wrote Mary Everest Boole in 1909. The tables are just as orderly in any base. Looking at a whole table, and at many bases together, shows the rules that make arithmetic work, not only the facts. Bases above 10 use the letters A, B, … for the digits 10, 11, …

Symmetry is commutativity

Every table is a mirror image of itself in its main diagonal: the entry for a, b is the one for b, a. That is the commutative law a + b = b + a, a × b = b × a. It is why it is enough to learn half of each table.

Patterns in the + table

Each row of the addition table is the row above it moved one place, because (a+1) + b = a + (b+1). Entries get a second digit, a carry, exactly below the diagonal where a + b = r − 1, the base minus one.

The last column of the × table

In base ten the multiples of 9 are 09, 18, 27, …, 81: the digits always add up to 9. The same holds in every base r for the multiples of r − 1: (r−1) × k is written with the digits k − 1 and r − k, because (r−1)k = (k−1)r + (r−k). In base 16, F × 7 = 69. The logic test checked every entry of both tables in every base from 2 to 36 (each read back is the true sum or product), along with the symmetry, the row shift, the carries and the last column.

Choose × and look at the last column in base 8, then base 12. Then look for the multiples of r + 1. What do their digits do?
